brief.head: A dish to start with
brief.text: India’s first im­por­tant soft­ware cen­tre by a global com­pany, as Ajay Shah re­calls it, was Texas Instruments’. It needed a satel­lite dish, and Montek Singh Ahluwalia helped win per­mis­sion. {028-S04}

brief.head: Hired by hand wave
brief.text: In a Kathmandu cor­ri­dor around 1974, Manmohan Singh told Vijay Kelkar, “So you will come to work with us, won’t you?” Kelkar felt obliged to say yes. {028-S21}

brief.head: Saamagri taiyaar hai
brief.text: Handing power to Atal Bihari Vajpayee in May 1996, Narasimha Rao told him the ma­te­rial for the nu­clear test was ready. His gov­ern­ment had left the de­ci­sion to the next. {028-S11}

brief.head: ‘Why me?’
brief.text: Almost every ac­com­plished woman Amit Varma in­vites on his pod­cast asks “Why me?”, he said. The men never do. He sees it as a left­over of a pa­tri­ar­chal past. {028-C10}

brief.head: Hello and goodbye
brief.text: In 2005 KP Krishnan burst into Ajay Shah’s fi­nance min­istry of­fice to say he had just joined. It was Shah’s last day there, and the day his mother died. {028-S22}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah pitch a web series
lead.head: Freedom, the second time round

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 28

body: Amit Varma wants a web se­ries made about India’s eco­nomic re­forms, and he knows how that sounds. “People will say, what a crazy geeky sub­ject,” he said. “And I’m like, yeah. But it’s in­cred­i­bly im­por­tant.”

The re­forms, from 1991 on­wards, got hun­dreds of mil­lions of peo­ple out of poverty. They were also, Varma said, the work of “a bunch of peo­ple who were fight­ing be­hind the scenes in what I think is a great free­dom move­ment”. {028-C01}
Like the orig­i­nal free­dom fight­ers, he said, they worked for prin­ci­ples that brought them no im­me­di­ate re­ward. He calls the se­ries *The Reformers*.
Ajay Shah, who had asked for one of the great­est sto­ries never told, added scenes of his own, and found him­self writ­ten into one.
## A cast of five
The pilot opens in the early 1960s in the rooms of Balbir Singh, an eco­nom­ics pro­fes­sor at St Stephen’s College, Delhi. A shy young Montek Singh Ahluwalia sits at the back.

Varma built the se­ries on five or six human sto­ries, the ones he knew best: Ahluwalia, PV Narasimha Rao, the econ­o­mists Isher Judge Ahluwalia and Padma Desai, and KP Krishnan of the fi­nance min­istry.
Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s thread is pa­tience. He came home in the late 1970s to a fi­nance min­istry post with no glory, and worked in the back­ground for years.

Varma cited the Abraham Lincoln line about spend­ing five of six hours sharp­en­ing the axe. When the 1991 cri­sis came, the axe was sharp, and the M doc­u­ment, a roadmap for re­form, was al­ready writ­ten. {028-C02}
Rao, in Varma’s telling, was a true be­liever and a man of deep learn­ing, not merely the politi­cian who man­aged other men’s re­forms.
Krishnan car­ries the 2008 cri­sis sea­son, and the image that opens and closes the se­ries: a man swim­ming laps, alone.
## Grace across elec­tions
Shah’s sto­ries turned on re­form as a relay. With elec­tions com­ing, P Chidambaram left in­fla­tion tar­get­ing to his suc­ces­sor rather than rush it through, and Arun Jaitley took it up.
“That’s the de­cency and grace by which we can build com­plex projects across elec­tions,” Shah said. {028-C05}
It also needs peo­ple who stay. “Ministers come, min­is­ters go,” Shah said; a pro­fes­sional elite must carry the mem­ory. That ca­pa­bil­ity, he warned, is not work­ing as it used to.
## Why they kept going

Varma asked how any­one keeps a sense of pur­pose while de­fend­ing ideas such as pos­i­tive-sum games and spon­ta­neous order, so eas­ily car­i­ca­tured as anti-poor. Yet these peo­ple, he said, gave decades to the long game, not col­umns from an arm­chair. {028-C07}

Shah’s first an­swer was wounded pride. India’s elite had be­lieved it was the post-colonial coun­try cer­tain to suc­ceed, the land of Tagore, Ramanujan, Nehru and Gandhi. The years from the 1962 China war to the Emergency, as East Asia grew rich, felt like a per­sonal af­front.
“You may have been a Marxist when you were young, but it ain’t work­ing and you have to change course,” he said. {028-C03}

His sec­ond an­swer was ideas. A sim­ple po­lit­i­cal-economy story, of the Mancur Olson kind, says firms be­hind 300 per cent tar­iffs would never let them fall. Yet du­ties fell year after year until 2007–08, be­cause the re­form­ers read and ar­gued.
Shah ended by rec­om­mend­ing Varma’s pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, as oral his­tory, then signed off as if he hosted it. Varma kept the fum­ble in.

second.label: Import licences
second.head: Stuck with the old model
second.deck: In 1983 an import licence locked Infosys into older, dearer computers

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Narayana Murthy’s import licence

body: In 1983 Narayana Murthy of Infosys wanted to im­port Data General com­put­ers, state of the art, with three re­mov­able hard drives of 200 MB each. “Can you imag­ine 200 whole MB?” Amit Varma asked. For months, Murthy made trips to the min­istry in Delhi for an im­port li­cence.

The li­cence came through just as Data General re­leased a newer ma­chine with 300 MB drives that was 30 per cent cheaper. {028-S03} But the li­cence was for one par­tic­u­lar model num­ber. Murthy could take the older, costlier ma­chine, or spend more months chas­ing an­other li­cence.
Ajay Shah added a con­nec­tion: his book pick in an ear­lier episode, *The Soul of a New Machine*, was about a de­sign project in­side Data General. {#soul}

quote.text: He can’t get that be­cause the li­cence is now for that par­tic­u­lar model num­ber.

third.head: Rao’s quiet word with Sony

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Narasimha Rao and Akio Morita

body: PV Narasimha Rao is often por­trayed as the man who han­dled the pol­i­tics while Manmohan Singh and Montek Singh Ahluwalia did the real work of re­form. Amit Varma dis­agrees. Rao, he said, was a true be­liever. {#believer}

His ev­i­dence is a scene he wants in the se­ries. Rao met Akio Morita, the chair­man of Sony, leaned over and al­most whis­pered that mil­lions of Indians dreamed of noth­ing greater than own­ing a Sony tele­vi­sion. Why not set up a fac­tory here? {028-S09}
Morita replied, in his gen­tle, un­der­stated way, that he would need so many li­cences he would never get them.
Rao leaned in fur­ther and, in a softer voice, said: “You just apply. Leave the rest to me.” Then, Varma said, “ev­ery­thing that kind of hap­pens, hap­pens.”

box.title: Where the scenes come from
box.text: Most of Amit Varma’s scenes come from books and his long in­ter­views: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s *Backstage*, Vinay Sitapati’s *Half-Lion*, and more than eight hours with KP Krishnan, which Varma calls an epic piece of oral his­tory. {028-R15}

sections.label: The pilot
sections.head: Marmite at St Stephen’s
sections.caption: the opening scene
body: Amit Varma’s se­ries, *The Reformers*, has a re­cur­ring shot of a man swim­ming laps, ex­plained only at the very end. The first episode proper opens on what looks like a vi­o­lent clash of colours. The cam­era pulls back. Someone is spread­ing Marmite on toast.
Ajay Shah ad­mit­ted that he hates Marmite. “So does the pro­tag­o­nist of this par­tic­u­lar chap­ter,” Varma said. {028-J02}
## A room in Rudra North

The cam­era pulls back fur­ther. It is the early 1960s, and the room is a suite in Rudra North at St Stephen’s College, Delhi, be­long­ing to Balbir Singh, an eco­nom­ics pro­fes­sor back from Oxford. Bade Ghulam Ali Khan is play­ing on the recorder, a lit­tle tin­nily. Balbir Singh likes sit­ting with young peo­ple and talk­ing about the world.
He wants to in­stil not rote learn­ing but a spirit of de­bate and in­quiry. That evening he talks music, not eco­nom­ics. At the back sits a quiet, slightly shy young Sardar: Montek Singh Ahluwalia.

Only then is the title re­vealed. The re­forms from 1991, Varma said, had great hu­man­i­tar­ian con­se­quences, and the peo­ple be­hind them worked for higher prin­ci­ples with no im­me­di­ate re­ward, much like the free­dom fight­ers be­fore them. {028-C01}
~ He would tell the story through five or six human sto­ries, the ones he knew, and ex­pected Shah to fill in some of the rest.

quote.text: A bunch of peo­ple who were fight­ing be­hind the scenes in what I think is a great free­dom move­ment.

sections.label: Montek’s years
sections.head: Eight days in the basement
sections.caption: Montek’s years in the background
body: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s mem­oir *Backstage* has a scene he barely un­der­scores, Amit Varma said, though Indian men will know why it is mov­ing. When he won a Rhodes Scholarship, he told his fa­ther in per­son. His fa­ther shook his hand, said con­grat­u­la­tions, and that was all. {028-S02}
Ajay Shah added a de­tail: the young man took the train to Bombay and went to Britain by ship. A ship, Varma said, gives you time to gather your thoughts.

After Oxford and years at the World Bank, Ahluwalia an­swered Manmohan Singh’s call, around 1977, to come home, and worked in the back­ground through the 1980s. Around 1990 he wrote the M doc­u­ment, a se­cret roadmap for re­form, be­fore the cri­sis hit.
## Locked in for India

When the re­form bud­get had to be pre­pared in se­crecy, 80 peo­ple, se­nior of­fi­cers among them, were taken to the base­ment of the fi­nance min­istry and kept there for eight days, with dor­mi­tory beds and food brought in. {028-S05} You could check out, Varma said, bor­row­ing from *Hotel California*, but you could never leave. {028-J05}

~ The work brought out un­ex­pected sides of peo­ple. After the gen­teel, soft-spoken Ahluwalia had an­swered ques­tion after ques­tion from the Joint Parliamentary Committee, an MP leav­ing the room gave a TV re­porter his ver­dict: “Sardarji bahut bolte hain.”

quote.text: All his fa­ther does is shake his hand and say con­grat­u­la­tions. And that’s it, be­cause we are just not so ex­pres­sive

sections.label: The prime minister
sections.head: Too learned for Delhi
sections.caption: PV Narasimha Rao’s many lives
body: PV Narasimha Rao, Amit Varma said, was not just a politi­cian who hap­pened to be there in 1991. Born around 1920, he knew some ten lan­guages, among them Telugu, Hindi, Marathi, Kannada, Urdu and Persian. When com­put­ers came to India in the 1980s, the min­is­ter taught him­self to code in COBOL and BASIC. {028-S07}
Delhi never took him se­ri­ously, Varma said. Its idea of re­fine­ment was how you speak English and how you hold your cup.

Vinay Sitapati, whose *Half-Lion* Varma calls fab­u­lous, wrote that Rao’s great­est qual­ity was his lone­li­ness. {028-S08} He got the top job after Rajiv Gandhi’s death partly by ac­ci­dent: Shankar Dayal Sharma turned it down, and Rao was seen not to be try­ing for it.
## A pyre and a relay

Rao died in 2004 an out­cast in his own party, and the Congress did not let his body come to Delhi for a state fu­neral. Television showed his half-burnt pyre in Hyderabad, with stray dogs at the re­mains. It makes Varma angry. {028-S10}

~ Ajay Shah added a story of grace across an elec­tion. With elec­tions com­ing, P Chidambaram wrote on file that in­fla­tion tar­get­ing should not be rushed through in a lame-duck administration’s last months, and left it to his suc­ces­sor. Arun Jaitley took it on. {028-S12}

quote.text: This was one of the great­est Indians of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury, whose ac­tions helped lift hun­dreds of mil­lions of peo­ple out of poverty.

portraits.caption: P. V. Narasimha Rao
portraits.credit: Christian Lambiotte - European Commission, CC BY 4.0

sections.label: Two women
sections.head: Breaking through, breaking out
sections.caption: Isher Judge Ahluwalia and Padma Desai
body: Isher Judge came from a con­ser­va­tive Sikh fam­ily and an all-girls Marwari school in Calcutta. She went to Presidency College and then to Delhi, where for a few months she strug­gled with English, the lan­guage of all the eco­nom­ics: her school had been Hindi medium. {028-S14}

She was sus­pi­cious of slick Delhi boys with ac­cents, but Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s sense of hu­mour won her over, and they courted watch­ing Godard, Truffaut and Bresson. She be­came, Amit Varma said, a very fine econ­o­mist. He re­grets leav­ing her mem­oir, *Breaking Through*, un­read until after she died.
## Credit by al­pha­bet

Padma Desai, Varma said, was a bril­liant econ­o­mist too often known only as Jagdish Bhagwati’s wife. {028-R04} Their 1968 book against India’s state-controlled sys­tem lists him first only by al­pha­bet­i­cal order, yet search re­sults credit him alone. She stud­ied the Soviet Union for years and wrote a re­spected 1989 book on per­e­stroika.
Trapped in an abu­sive mar­riage and re­fused a di­vorce, she used one of the legal grounds avail­able, change of re­li­gion, and con­verted to Christianity to marry Bhagwati. {028-S15}

~ Ajay Shah re­called Bhagwati telling a din­ner table that his brother, PN Bhagwati, had found the cou­ple “liv­ing in sin” and warned that it was a crime under the IPC, “so just be care­ful”. {028-J11}

quote.text: The women are dou­bly re­mark­able be­cause women are not in this game at all.

sections.label: The civil servant
sections.head: Opposition, by arrangement
sections.caption: KP Krishnan’s stories
body: KP Krishnan is the hero of the sea­son Amit Varma would give to the 2008 fi­nan­cial cri­sis, the first India faced as part of the global econ­omy. Varma recorded more than eight hours with him, an epic piece of oral his­tory, he said, that Ajay Shah made pos­si­ble. {028-R15}

Krishnan’s sto­ries were also about pol­i­tics. The New Pension Scheme, pre­pared under the Vajpayee gov­ern­ment, was em­braced by Manmohan Singh’s. Across the table sat Sushma Swaraj, now in op­po­si­tion. She called it won­der­ful and good for the coun­try, warned that she would have to op­pose it in Parliament, and then laid out, step by step, how to get it passed. {028-S18}
## A lost decade

Then the mo­men­tum broke, by ac­ci­dent. After the Bombay at­tacks of 2008, Varma said, draw­ing on Puja Mehra’s *The Lost Decade*, P Chidambaram was moved to the home min­istry and Pranab Mukherjee ended up at fi­nance. He was “a com­plete dis­as­ter as a fi­nance min­is­ter”, Varma said, bring­ing in ret­ro­spec­tive tax­a­tion. {028-S19}
~ Krishnan, a man of deep in­tegrity, did not hold the in­flu­en­tial posts he should have after 2015, Varma said. Many re­form­ers, he felt, were left out in the cold.

quote.text: Let me tell you some­thing, in pub­lic, be­cause I’m in the op­po­si­tion, if you bring it to par­lia­ment, I will have to op­pose it.
quote.who: Sushma Swaraj, as told by Amit Varma

sections.label: More anecdotes
sections.head: Opening the oil tap, slowly
sections.caption: Vijay Kelkar’s petroleum years
body: A story that means a lot to Ajay Shah is Vijay Kelkar’s jour­ney at the pe­tro­leum min­istry. When Kelkar ar­rived as an ad­viser, the state had a com­plete mo­nop­oly on ev­ery­thing pe­tro­leum: ex­plo­ration, ex­trac­tion, re­fin­ing, dis­tri­bu­tion and petro­chem­i­cals.

Kelkar, the econ­o­mist, un­der­stood the sector’s fun­da­men­tal eco­nom­ics. Lavraj Kumar, the sec­re­tary, knew how to work the bu­reau­cratic and po­lit­i­cal ma­chine. Both be­lieved there was no case for state mo­nop­o­lies. When Lavraj Kumar’s time ended, Kelkar, though not from the IAS, be­came sec­re­tary and stayed six years across gov­ern­ments.
Exploration, ex­trac­tion, re­fin­ing and petro­chem­i­cals be­came pri­vate. Distribution, Shah said, fum­bled. {028-S23}
## Institutional mem­ory

Such jour­neys take many years, Shah said, and that ca­pa­bil­ity is no longer work­ing as it used to. Ministers come and go; what car­ries knowl­edge across, he said, is a pro­fes­sional elite that sus­tains and pro­tects its own. {028-C06}

Even the fi­nance min­is­ter had to re­cruit al­lies one at a time. Around 1991–92, Amit Varma said, Manmohan Singh held on to Naushad Forbes’s hand after a meet­ing with in­dus­try lead­ers and whis­pered: “Tell the world ev­ery­thing you said today in­side here.” {028-S24}
~ For Shah, Steven Spielberg’s *Lincoln* was an eye-opener: it skips the bat­tles to stay with the legal fight over one amend­ment. “My God, it is great sto­ry­telling,” he said.

quote.text: Ministers come, min­is­ters go, but you need this sta­bil­ity of the pro­fes­sional elite pub­lic pol­icy in India

And yet, not for years, but for decades, these peo­ple don’t do what peo­ple like me do, write col­umns and be arm­chair colum­nists, but for years and decades these peo­ple de­vote their lives to play­ing this long game.

p3.title: Scenes for the series
p3.deck: Four stories the hosts would film, and what each one teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s recurring scene, and the man in the water
stories.head: Laps first, cabinet later
body: Every sea­son of Amit Varma’s imag­ined se­ries is punc­tu­ated by one image. From high above, a tiny glis­ten­ing blue speck sits in a mass of land. The cam­era drops until the speck be­comes a large swim­ming pool, and the specks in it be­come the arms of a man swim­ming from one end to the other.

The scene would re­turn in quiet mo­ments across nine or ten sea­sons. {#seasons} Someone comes to talk to the swim­mer; he says some­thing; they leave; he keeps swim­ming. The au­di­ence would not know what it means until the se­ries ends, on the same shot.

The swim­mer is KP Krishnan, for whom swim­ming is a non-negotiable part of his reg­i­men. During a cab­i­net meet­ing that went on and on, he asked if he could step out for an hour. {#cabinet} Asked what was so ur­gent, he said he wanted to swim, and then come back.

Varma learnt this first-hand. His in­ter­view with Krishnan, more than eight hours long, could have been recorded in three ses­sions but took four. {#sessions} One of them, at a con­fer­ence in Kochi, ran into his swim­ming time of six o’clock. Krishnan had checked out the pool ear­lier. “Sir, please go,” Varma told him.
He re­spects that, Varma said: con­vic­tion and force of will about one’s own rou­tines, not just the larger things.
The scene, he said, is a great metaphor for the reformer’s life: you are swim­ming alone. {028-S01}
~ “Someone in­ter­rupts you at one point and you send him away, you con­tinue to swim,” Varma said. “And right at the end, the last scene, you’re still swim­ming alone.”
stories.why: Reform is a long swim taken alone. Varma mar­velled that such peo­ple gave not years but decades to a cause few un­der­stood, in­stead of writ­ing col­umns from an arm­chair, as he does. {028-C07}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on KP Krishnan’s swim

stories.kicker: How the Lehman crisis emptied a Delhi stage
stories.head: And then there were none
body: The sea­son on the 2008 cri­sis, Amit Varma said, would open in a dimly lit base­ment in Delhi with no phone sig­nal. On stage, Ajay Shah is mod­er­at­ing a panel: KP Krishnan of the fi­nance min­istry, RBI gov­er­nor Subbarao and Bhave of SEBI.

A man walks up and whis­pers in Krishnan’s ear. Krishnan gets up and leaves. Another whis­pers to Subbarao, who leaves, then an­other to Bhave. “And you’re sud­denly mod­er­at­ing a con­ver­sa­tion with no par­tic­i­pants,” Varma said. {028-S16}
Lehman Brothers had col­lapsed. Finance min­is­ter P Chidambaram, un­able to reach any of the three on their phones, had got calls through to their driv­ers in­stead.
~ The au­di­ence, Varma added, would not have minded, “be­cause you’re on stage and you’re so beau­ti­ful”. {028-J15}
stories.why: When a cri­sis breaks, the peo­ple run­ning the sys­tem van­ish from pub­lic view. How they han­dled 2008, Varma said, is in­cred­i­bly in­spir­ing, and de­serves a sea­son of its own, per­haps two.
stories.postscript: Shah’s own mem­ory of the night be­fore: hours watch­ing the price of ICICI Bank’s ADR in New York. It barely moved. {028-C11}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the panel that vanished

stories.kicker: KP Krishnan’s two-slide pitch to Pranab Mukherjee
stories.head: Two slides and a postcard
body: KP Krishnan wanted an im­por­tant fi­nan­cial-sector re­form, and Pranab Mukherjee’s in­stinc­tive so­cial­ist, 1970s self, Amit Varma said, would have re­volted at it. So Krishnan brought him a pre­sen­ta­tion of two slides.
The first was a post­card to Mukherjee from a con­stituent in Bengal, Sharmishtha Bandopadhyay, which he had read out. Her life sav­ings were gone, and it was up to him to do some­thing. {028-S20}

By the end Mukherjee was fu­ri­ous. “Why are you read­ing this out for me? What do you want?” he de­manded. {#furious} Krishnan said the cur­rent sys­tem ruins com­mon peo­ple like her, and pro­posed the re­form. Mukherjee ap­proved it on the spot.
~ Varma loves the way Krishnan, a side player in one of the min­istries in 1991, worked out how to present such re­forms to politi­cians so they hap­pened right away.
stories.why: Financial re­form bores most au­di­ences, Varma said, yet it shapes everyone’s life. Krishnan’s trick was to start with one named per­son the sys­tem had ru­ined. Reformers and sto­ry­tellers alike, Varma said, need such ways to tell it. {028-C08}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the postcard that won over Pranab

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a trade ban you could smell
stories.head: Eau de licence raj
body: Ajay Shah had the story from NK Singh. In an el­e­va­tor at the IMF, one man turned round with­out look­ing and said to the per­son be­hind him: “You’re from India, aren’t you?” He was right. How did he know?

The an­swer lay in the suit. Anyone who is, in Shah’s words, “an un­for­tu­nate owner of a thing called a suit” must have it dry-cleaned, and dry clean­ing sig­nals class, since the poor can­not af­ford it. {028-J07}

India had banned im­ports of the cor­rect dry-cleaning flu­ids as lux­u­ries. Indian dry clean­ers used bad petro­chem­i­cals in­stead, which left a dis­tinc­tive stink. {028-S06} A suit with that smell, Shah said, be­longed to some­one from India.
~ Later he called the story “the psy­chic dy­na­mite that makes things hap­pen”.
stories.why: Protectionism left traces on or­di­nary life, down to the smell of a suit. Shah counts such small hu­mil­i­a­tions, with the bruise of watch­ing East Asia grow rich, among the forces that made India’s elite re­think. {028-C03}
stories.postscript: Varma wants one scene in the se­ries set in a dry cleaner’s.

quiz.q: Why could Narayana Murthy not buy Data General’s newer, cheaper computer in 1983?
quiz.a: His im­port li­cence was for one par­tic­u­lar model num­ber, the older ma­chine.

quiz.q: What gave away an Indian in an IMF elevator, in the story NK Singh told Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: The stink of bad petro­chem­i­cals Indian dry clean­ers used after fluid im­ports were banned.

quiz.q: Which two computer languages did PV Narasimha Rao teach himself to code fluently in?
quiz.a: COBOL and BASIC, after com­put­ers came to India in the 1980s.

quiz.q: How did Padma Desai free herself from an abusive first marriage to marry Jagdish Bhagwati?
quiz.a: She con­verted to Christianity, since change of re­li­gion was a legal ground for di­vorce.

quiz.q: What did Arun Jaitley say when KP Krishnan urged him to think harder about inflation targeting?
quiz.a: Two of India’s finest legal and eco­nomic minds had agreed: who was he to dis­agree?

quiz.q: Lehman had collapsed and nobody’s phone worked in the basement. How did Chidambaram reach his officials?
quiz.a: He got calls through to their driv­ers, and some­one whis­pered to each on stage.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 28. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: P. V. Narasimha Rao (Christian Lambiotte - European Commission, CC BY 4.0); Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0); Manmohan Singh (Prime Minister’s Office, GODL-India); Arun Jaitley (Ministry of Defence, GODL-India); Sushma Swaraj (U.S. Department of State from United States, public domain); Pranab Mukherjee (US Treasury Department, public domain); Steven Spielberg (Raph_PH, CC BY 4.0).

shelf.title: Backstage
shelf.creator: Montek Singh Ahluwalia
shelf.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s mem­oir of the re­form years, full of human de­tail about work­ing in­side the sys­tem and con­crete ex­am­ples of how li­cens­ing stran­gled Indian en­ter­prise.

shelf.title: Half-Lion
shelf.creator: Vinay Sitapati
shelf.why: Sitapati’s bi­og­ra­phy of Narasimha Rao, which shows him as a great man of learn­ing and con­stant rein­ven­tion who staked his po­lit­i­cal cap­i­tal on the 1991 re­forms, not just a politi­cian who hap­pened to be there.

shelf.title: Breaking Through
shelf.creator: Isher Judge Ahluwalia
shelf.why: A beau­ti­ful book about a Hindi-medium girl who be­came a fine econ­o­mist.

shelf.title: Breaking Out
shelf.creator: Padma Desai
shelf.why: The story of a re­mark­able econ­o­mist and a strong woman who often goes un­cred­ited.

shelf.title: The Lost Decade
shelf.creator: Puja Mehra
shelf.why: Puja Mehra’s ac­count of how India’s growth stalled after 2008, through de­ci­sions like ret­ro­spec­tive tax­a­tion and the reshuf­fle that made Pranab Mukherjee fi­nance min­is­ter.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: The Struggle and the Promise
shelf.creator: Naushad Forbes
shelf.why: Written by a busi­ness leader who backed re­form pub­licly when few oth­ers did.

shelf.title: The Logic of Collective Action
shelf.creator: Mancur Olson
shelf.why: Olson’s ac­count of ‘con­cen­trated ben­e­fits and dif­fuse costs’: why small, or­gan­ised in­ter­est groups beat the large, un­or­gan­ised pub­lic.

shelf.title: Lincoln
shelf.creator: Steven Spielberg
shelf.why: An eye-opener for Ajay.

shelf.title: Kohrra
shelf.creator: Sudip Sharma
shelf.why: Amit calls it a mar­vel­lous se­ries and was so im­pressed by Suvinder Vicky’s lead per­for­mance that he wants him to play Montek.

shelf.title: Milestone
shelf.creator: Ivan Ayr
shelf.why: The film where Suvinder Vicky first im­pressed Danish Husain, back­ing up Amit’s cast­ing choice.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s long-form pod­cast of three-to-eight-hour deep dives, con­ver­sa­tions no gate­keeper would have com­mis­sioned, which have be­come an oral his­tory of India; its show notes list every book men­tioned.

shelf.title: The Soul of a New Machine
shelf.why: A jour­nal­ist em­bed­ded with a Data General team build­ing a CPU takes you into the minds of the en­gi­neers and their leader, Tom West, in­clud­ing the empti­ness once the quest was over.

shelf.title: The 1991 Project
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan’s trea­sure trove of chron­i­cles and oral his­to­ries of the 1991 re­forms, in­clud­ing the leg­endary ‘M document’.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Episode 285, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
shelf.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s first-hand ac­count of his decades in the re­form en­gine room and the ‘silent revolution’ that built up from the late 1970s.

shelf.title: The Forgotten Greatness of PV Narasimha Rao (Episode 283, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
shelf.why: Vinay Sitapati on why Narasimha Rao de­serves much of the credit for the 1991 re­forms, and on the re­form­ers around him.

shelf.title: India’s Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane
shelf.why: Ajay and Renuka Sane on the old ver­sus new pen­sion scheme: a bi­par­ti­san re­form built by a small in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity, and how in­sti­tu­tional mem­ory van­ished once that com­mu­nity dis­persed.

shelf.title: Naushad Forbes Wants to Fix India (Episode 282, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Naushad Forbes
shelf.why: A busi­ness leader who backed re­form when there was al­most no pub­lic sup­port, show­ing that re­form­ers in­side gov­ern­ment needed out­siders to sell the ideas.

shelf.title: India’s Lost Decade (Episode 116, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Puja Mehra
shelf.why: Puja Mehra on what went wrong after 2008 and how the re­form era un­rav­elled, a com­pan­ion to her book The Lost Decade.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: Danish Husain and the Multiverse of Culture (Episode 359, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Danish Husain
shelf.why: Where Amit learned that Danish shared his ad­mi­ra­tion for Vicky’s act­ing.

shelf.title: One Bad Law Goes, but Women Remain Second-Class Citizens
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s 2018 col­umn on the now-scrapped adul­tery law, which treated a wife as her husband’s prop­erty, and on other IPC pro­vi­sions that still do.

shelf.title: Seven Stories That Should Be Films (Episode 23, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The first of the show’s se­ries of true sto­ries the hosts would turn into films, and Amit’s favourite episode at the time.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: Math Is Better Than the Brigadier’s Girlfriend (Episode 15, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: An early episode that the hosts cite as in-person col­lab­o­ra­tion at its best, and as back­ground for the Data General con­nec­tion Ajay draws later.

laughs.text: After Ajay ad­mits his taste in films is a 13-year-old’s love of spec­ta­cle, Amit sums up the pair: ‘You are the kind of per­son who likes to blow things up, and I’m the kind of per­son who wants to curl up in a cor­ner and cry.’

The pilot’s open­ing shot looks like a vi­o­lent clash of colours until the cam­era pulls back to show some­one spread­ing Marmite on toast. Ajay ad­mits he hates Marmite, and Amit says ‘So does the pro­tag­o­nist of this par­tic­u­lar chap­ter.’
Ajay on the Texas Instruments satel­lite-dish saga: ‘Voluntary trans­ac­tions by con­sent­ing adults were very com­pli­cated.’

After Montek, a gen­teel and soft-spoken man, fielded ques­tion after ques­tion from the Joint Parliamentary Committee, a TV re­porter asked an MP leav­ing the room how it went. His an­swer: ‘Sardarji bahut bolte hain.’ It also be­came a chap­ter title.

Ajay sets up the dry-cleaning story with ‘if you are a male who is an un­for­tu­nate owner of a thing called a suit’, not­ing that dry clean­ing is how you sig­nal class, since poor peo­ple can’t af­ford it.

On Shankar Dayal Sharma turn­ing down the top job to be­come President later, Amit para­phrases: ‘I can chill and be in the Rashtrapati Bhavan. Not in so many words, ob­vi­ously, be­cause I don’t think Mr. Sharma would have said I can chill.’

Ajay on the RBI’s ori­gins: the 1934 Act called it a tem­po­rary mea­sure be­cause the British ‘had no idea what they were doing’, so ‘the con­cept of the Reserve Bank of India re­ally only began in 2015.’

Ajay re­calls Jagdish Bhagwati telling a din­ner table that his brother, PN Bhagwati, found out Jagdish and Padma Desai were ‘liv­ing in sin’ and grum­bled that it was a crime under the IPC, ‘so just be care­ful.’

Ajay calls Isher telling him his ar­tic­u­la­tion was like young Montek’s ‘the sweet­est thing that any­body ever said to me.’ Amit: ‘I’m sure young Montek’s hu­mour was bet­ter than yours.’ Ajay: ‘No doubt.’

As the pan­el­lists van­ish one by one dur­ing the Lehman cri­sis, Amit says the au­di­ence doesn’t mind ‘be­cause you’re on stage and you’re so beau­ti­ful and they’re just look­ing at you lost in rap­ture.’
Ending his rec­om­men­da­tion of Amit’s pod­cast, Ajay signs off with ‘we’re at the end of this episode of The Seen and the Unseen.’ Amit: ‘We won’t edit that out. It’s a very nice fum­ble.’

The open­ing scene is set in econ­o­mist Balbir Singh’s suite in Rudra North at St Stephen’s in the early 1960s. Bade Ghulam Ali Khan plays tin­nily on a recorder while the Oxford-returned pro­fes­sor talks music with stu­dents, and a shy young Montek sits at the back.
On the 80 of­fi­cials locked in the fi­nance min­istry base­ment for eight days, Amit bor­rows the Hotel California line: ‘you can check out but you can never leave.’

Ajay asks whether Narasimha Rao was a Gorbachev fig­ure: deeply knowl­edge­able and also a mas­ter of the in­trigue needed to win and hold power. Amit says he doesn’t know enough about Gorbachev to judge.
Isher and Montek’s courtship: watch­ing European films by Godard, Truffaut and Bresson to­gether.
Ajay de­scribes Manmohan Singh re­cruit­ing Vijay Kelkar in a Kathmandu cor­ri­dor with ‘a Jedi hand wave’, the Star Wars mind trick, after which Kelkar sim­ply felt obliged to say yes.
